did_you_know.text: The phrase “advanced in days” is a biblical way of saying that Abraham had reached a very old age. It suggests not only many years, but also a life full of experience and deeds.
Placing a hand under the thigh was part of an ancient oath ritual. Its exact meaning is uncertain, but it clearly expressed a serious commitment.
Abraham asks for a wife who is not a Canaanite. In this way, he seeks to preserve his family and cultural connections.
The servant asks a practical question: What if the woman refuses to move to Canaan? Abraham makes clear that Isaac himself must not return to the land Abraham left.
Abraham believes that the God who guided him in the past will guide this new mission as well. That is why he mentions both the promise and the angel.
“Aram-Naharaim” means “Aram of the two rivers,” usually referring to a region of Mesopotamia between the Euphrates and Tigris. It was a long journey north from the area of Hebron or the Negev.
Wells were central places in ancient town life: people drew water there, met others, and sometimes formed family connections. The servant arrives at the time when the women come to draw water.
The servant does not choose Rebecca by appearance alone; he looks for generosity and a willingness to help. Watering ten camels was a demanding task, so the sign required action, not just words.
The story emphasizes that Rebecca arrives before the servant has even finished praying. This creates a sense of a swift and precise answer from divine providence.
The jar on Rebecca’s shoulder shows that she carried the water herself, without a small vessel or someone else’s help. The well was below ground level, so one had to go down to it and climb back up.
Rebecca respectfully calls the servant “my lord,” even though she does not yet know who he is. Such courtesy was an important part of hospitality in the ancient world.
Rebecca does not stop after giving the servant one drink; she offers to water the camels until they finish. She turns a small act of kindness into a long and demanding effort.
The servant is “watching in amazement,” waiting to see whether the sign will come true. The story pauses the action for a moment to heighten the suspense.
A “bekah” was an ancient unit of weight, not the name of a modern coin. The weight of the bracelets is given separately to show that they were valuable and significant gifts.
Rebecca offers not only a place to sleep, but also straw and feed for the camels. Hospitality in that period meant caring for both people and their animals.
The servant refuses to eat before explaining the purpose of his mission. This shows how strongly he places his duty before his personal comfort.
The list of sheep, cattle, silver, gold, and camels presents wealth in ancient terms. Such property was both a source of power and a sign of social status.
The phrase “I will turn to the right or to the left” means that if the family refuses, the servant will continue searching elsewhere. It is a vivid way of saying, “I will find another option.”
Gifts for the bride and her family were part of the ancient process of forming an official bond between families. They expressed respect, seriousness, and agreement to the marriage.
The family does not decide entirely on its own; they call Rebecca and ask her directly. Her brief answer, “I will go,” presents her as someone who makes her own decision.
Beer-lahai-roi is the place where Hagar previously encountered the angel of the Lord in chapter 16. Mentioning it connects Hagar’s story with Isaac’s story.
The verb “lasuach” is sometimes translated as “to pray” or “to meditate,” but its exact meaning is uncertain. In any case, Isaac goes alone into the field at evening, just before meeting Rebecca.
